newsitem.title: JAPAN: Several big Japan insurers to boost dividends.
newsitem.headline: Several big Japan insurers to boost dividends.

text.p: Despite a poor investment environment due to low interest rates and a weak stock market, several major Japanese life insurers said they will boost dividends as a result of improved balance sheets.
They said that restructuring efforts in the business year which ended in March had helped their bottom line.

Nippon Life Insurance Co, Japan's biggest life insurer, said on Wednesday that it would increase ordinary dividends to be paid to individual policyholders for the 1996/97 fiscal year for the first time in seven years.

A company spokesman said that while yields on investments remained low in 1996/97 due to low interest rates and declines in stock prices, Nippon Life was profitable because it cut operating costs and wrote off problem loans.
A spokesman at Meiji Life Insurance Co said the insurer would also increase its dividends because of cost-cutting efforts. Neither would comment on the extent of the increase.
Industry sources said other big life insurers such as Dai-ichi Mutual Life Insurance Co and Sumitomo Life Insurance Co were also expected to increase their ordinary dividends.
But the increase will be different for each company, depending on their financial strength, they added.

Makoto Fukuda, director of the Banking Bureau's Insurance Department, told a parliamentary committee on Wednesday that the restructuring efforts would help the industry overcome a tough business climate caused by ultra-low interest rates.
Japan's official discount rate -- that at which it lends to commercial banks -- has been kept at a record-low 0.5 percent since September 1995 in an effort to boost economic recovery.
Japan's eight biggest life insurers are scheduled to announce their 1996/97 earnings on Monday and details of any dividend increases would be made then.
Eight medium-sized life insurers will announce their business results on Tuesday.
Japan's financial markets will closely watch the results because of the failure of Nissan Mutual Life Insurance Co in April, analysts said.
"I will focus on the difference in the size of assets between 1996/97 and 1995/96," said Koya Hasegawa, an analyst at Nikko Research Centre.
"The business results are expected to show a widening gap in financial strength among the insurers."

The insurance firms cut their guaranteed rate of return in April 1996 on investments they managed for penson funds, which resulted in a withdrawal of pension fund management contracts in the first half of 1996/97.
That resulted in seven of the eight biggest life insurers experiencing a drop in assets in the first half for the first time since World War Two, analysts said.
The exception was Nippon Life.
But industry sources said the cancellations also had a positive impact as they helped narrow the negative spread between low investment yields and already promised payouts.

The negative spread has been a serious headache for the insurers since the bursting of the late 1980s "economic bubble" of inflated asset prices when the insurers sold policies with high guaranteed rates of return.
But once the economy slowed and interest rates fell, the insurers had trouble generating revenue to meet the guaranteed returns, the sources said.

The sources and analysts also said that stock price falls in 1996/97 forced the life insurers to post appraisal losses on their shareholdings, forcing some insurers to sell profitable securities such as stocks, bonds and foreign securities in order to cover the appraisal losses.

As a result, some insurers may have lost most of their unrealised shareholding profits, which would weaken their financial sturdiness as the unrealised profits had been used as a source of funds to cover unexpected financial losses and problem loan write-offs, they said.
